newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuanian finance minister sees growth, sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: Lithuanian finance minister sees growth, sell-offs.

text.p: New Lithuanian Finance Minister Algirdas Shemeta said on Wednesday he was optimistic over growth prospects for the Baltic state and voiced support for the privatisation of big state companies.

Shemeta,34, was appointed by President Algirdas Brazauskas to replace previous finance minister Rolandas Matiliauskas, forced to resign last month over allegations he took a soft loan from a troubled bank.
"I think the economic perspectives for the country for 1997 are quite good," Shemeta told Reuters in a brief interview after his appointment.
"Very preliminary data show that (1996) gross domestic product (GDP) growth was between 3.6 and four percent," he added.
"I think that the tendency for economic growth will remain in 1997 and will even increase," he said.

Shemeta, an economist and mathematician, worked most recently as the head of the securities commission. He expressed full support for right-wing Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius' plans to speed up privatisation and attract more foreign investment.
"I think that we need to privatise quickly big infrastructure and public utilities companies," Shemeta said.
"I am for rapid, sensible and open privatisation, attracting foreign investors, foreign advisers and foreign investment banks," he added.
Vagnorius leads a coalition which swept a party of former Communists out of power in autumn last year.
Lithuania launched market reforms after it split from the former Soviet Union in 1991 but under the previous left-wing government failed to tackle the privatisation of large state-owned firms.
Shemeta also said he would try to bring order to the tax administration to boost government revenues and make sure that the 1997 budget was carried out as planned.

Shemeta's role will also be key as Lithuania plans to change its monetary system, involving ending the currency board system of managing its money supply and exchange rate. The system allows for money supply changes only in direct relation to foreign currency reserves at a fixed exchange rate, currently at four litas to one dollar.
Officials have repeatedly assured the change will not lead to a litas devaluation but Deutsche Bank has predicted a 25 percent fall in the unit after the end of the currency board.
The central bank has said it plans to maintain the fixed rate but wants to manage monetary policy with traditional methods such as money market interventions and interest rate changes.
